source.title: Understanding Generalization in Quantum Machine Learning with Margins

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present, including appendices; figure values are partly legible in the supplied text.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether margin-based measurements track generalization in quantum models, using different measurements and models from the mapped versions.
record.gate_note: The paper's claim that QCNNs overfit randomized labels cites Gil-Fuster et al. (2024); it is not this study's own result. The study reports its own margin, test-accuracy, and generalization-gap results for quantum models, which do not test the specific mapped versions.
record.test_reason: The study reports quantum-classifier margin and embedding results, which measure different constructs and systems from V1–V8. Its statements about fitting random labels cite prior work; its own reported results do not establish the memorization-and-generalization conjunction in V1. Margin correlations do not test magnitude-aware sharpness in V7.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate: the authors propose a quantum margin bound, find margin metrics more predictive of generalization gaps than parameter-count metrics in their experiments, and associate larger embedding trace distances with larger margins and better test accuracy. The theoretical trace-distance result bounds the achievable margin mean; it does not by itself guarantee improved held-out accuracy.
record.recipe_differences: Quantum convolutional neural networks and quantum margin/trace-distance measurements; the mapped versions concern classical networks, optimizers, regularization, sharpness, or example removal.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcomes vary with label-randomization level, QCNN layer count, variational ansatz, embedding method, and dataset.

fits_no_version.finding: Inverse margin metrics tracked generalization gaps better than parameter-count metrics across the tested quantum circuit depths, label-corruption levels, and ansätze.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In these quantum-classifier experiments, margin metrics predict generalization gaps better than total or effective parameter counts.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing label corruption lowered quantum-phase test accuracy and shifted margins toward smaller values; fully randomized labels yielded 0.25 test accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For the tested quantum phase classifiers, greater label corruption accompanies smaller margins and lower test accuracy.

fits_no_version.finding: Across the three image datasets, fixed, trainable, and neural quantum embeddings exhibited progressively larger trace distances, larger margin means, and better test accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In the tested quantum image classifiers, embedding methods with greater class distinguishability are associated with larger margins and higher test accuracy.

record.problems: Key plotted values are not fully recoverable from the supplied figure text. The main QCNN experiments use 20 training points and average over 15 repetitions; exact uncertainty intervals are not reported in the provided text. Some conclusions about overfitting random labels are cited from prior work rather than newly established here.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows extracted. Figure 4's individual dataset-by-embedding accuracy assignments are unrecoverable from the flattened supplied text; the available values are noted without assigning them to specific cells.

untested.parts: The same classical architectures and recipes fitting random labels nearly perfectly while generalizing on natural labels; own random-label training-fit results are not reported.
Test error as width increases beyond the zero-training-error threshold.
Classical convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD under comparable tuning conditions.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and recipe adaptations.
Dropout effects, training-set-size dependence, and interaction with augmentation or weight decay.
Magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and its ranking against norm- and margin-based measures.
Removing highly memorized training examples versus removing equally many random examples.

record.verdict_notes: No verdict labels apply to V1–V8. Chance-level random-label test accuracy alone does not establish memorization capacity. Figure 4's caption supplies dataset order and panel identities, permitting accuracy assignments more specific than the record allows.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not report that its own models fit randomized labels nearly perfectly while also generalizing on natural labels.
No one-hidden-layer ReLU width sweep is reported.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison is reported.
No adaptive-versus-SGD optimizer generalization comparison is reported.
No large-batch versus small-batch comparison is reported.
The study measures margins, not magnitude-aware weight perturbation sharpness, and does not compare that sharpness measure with norm- or margin-based measures.
No memorized-example removal experiment is reported.

rows.subject: 8-qubit QCNNs
rows.operation_detail: Measured margin distributions and test accuracy across label-corruption levels and layer counts.
rows.measure: Test accuracy and margin distribution; the supplied figure text lists test accuracy as 0.81, 0.84, and 0.85 for the three layer counts, respectively.
rows.value: Figure 1 lists test accuracy 0.81, 0.84, and 0.85; the text says deeper QCNNs tend to achieve higher test accuracy when labels are not completely randomized.
rows.note: The figure labels list three accuracies, but the supplied text does not unambiguously map their order to layer counts. The text describes the trend qualitatively.
rows.check: Natural-label test accuracies alone do not establish V1's conjunction with near-perfect random-label training fit. These are quantum classifiers on quantum phase data.

rows.note: The supplied figure text does not unambiguously map the three accuracy labels to layer counts.
rows.check: Partial label corruption, test accuracy, and margins do not measure any listed version.

rows.subject: 8-qubit QCNNs
rows.operation_detail: Measured test accuracy and margin distributions with fully randomized labels.
rows.measure: Test accuracy; figure labels give 0.25 for all three layer counts.
rows.note: The text says accuracy declines as randomization increases; 0.25 is the stated chance-level value for this four-class task.
rows.check: The 0.25 test accuracy is chance for four classes, but no corresponding near-perfect random-label training accuracy is reported. Change observed to cannot_determine relative to the listed versions.

rows.subject: QCNNs
rows.operation_detail: Compared generalization gap, inverse median margin, and square root of effective parameters across layer counts.
rows.measure: Generalization gap peaks at five layers before slightly decreasing; median margin captures the peak, while effective parameters increase monotonically.
rows.value: Qualitative result as stated in Section 3.2; plotted values are figure only.
rows.note: A quantum-model margin result; it does not measure magnitude-aware sharpness.
rows.check: Measures inverse margins and effective parameter counts, not magnitude-aware sharpness. A depth sweep also does not test V2's width claim.

rows.operation_detail: Compared margin and effective-parameter metrics as label randomization increased.

conditions.value: inverse median margin and square root of effective parameters

rows.measure: The margin metric captures the rising generalization gap; effective parameters show an inverse trend.
rows.value: Qualitative result as stated in Section 3.2; plotted values are figure only.
rows.note: The study reports a qualitative comparison without numerical values in the text.
rows.check: Margin-versus-parameter correlations under label corruption do not measure V7's sharpness relationship.

rows.operation_detail: Compared generalization gap, margin, and effective parameters across variational ansätze.

conditions.value: QCNN, QCNN with shared parameters, and Strongly Entangling Layers

rows.measure: Margin reflects the rising generalization gap as expressibility decreases; effective parameters show an inverse trend.
rows.value: Qualitative result as stated in Section 3.2; plotted values are figure only.
rows.note: The study reports the comparison across ansätze, but not numerical values in the text.
rows.check: The subject should include all three compared ansätze: QCNN, shared-parameter QCNN, and Strongly Entangling Layers. This is neither a classical convolutional-versus-fully-connected comparison nor a sharpness experiment.

rows.subject: QCNNs
rows.operation_detail: Compared margin-based and parameter-based metrics for association with generalization gap.

conditions.value: margin Q1, median, mean; parameters; effective parameters at 10^-1 and 10^-2

rows.measure: Margin-based metrics show stronger mutual information and Kendall rank correlation with generalization gap than parameter-based metrics.
rows.value: Higher correlations for margin-based metrics; precise values are figure only.
rows.note: The text states the direction of the comparison but gives no exact correlation values.
rows.check: Margin metrics outperform parameter-count metrics; magnitude-aware sharpness and norm-based comparators are not evaluated. The swept models include multiple quantum ansätze, not only QCNNs.
